promptText: Why doesn't reactive programming make an individual request's latency lower?
options: Because a single request's latency is unchanged or even slightly worse due to callback and scheduler overhead - the win is handling far higher concurrency with a bounded thread count, not per-request speed
Because the JVM disables JIT compilation for any code running inside a Mono/Flux chain
Because Mono and Flux always execute on a single dedicated background thread that is inherently slower than a platform thread
Because reactive frameworks add a mandatory network round trip for every operator in the chain
explanation: The chapter frames it as 'threads are the scarce resource, not requests': reactive trades a small latency/overhead cost from callbacks and thread hops for the ability to handle vastly more concurrent I/O-bound operations with a fixed thread count.

promptText: Under the Reactive Streams specification, what mechanism stops a fast Publisher from flooding a slow Subscriber by default?
options: The JVM's garbage collector pauses producer threads once heap pressure crosses a threshold
The pull-based Subscription.request(n) call: the publisher must never emit more items than the subscriber has explicitly asked for
TCP-level flow control alone, with no cooperation required from the Publisher implementation
Every onNext call blocks the producer thread until the subscriber acknowledges receipt
explanation: request(n) is the entire backpressure protocol built into the spec: nothing flows until the consumer asks for it, which is what separates Reactive Streams from a plain unbounded push-based Observer.

promptText: Why is Mono<T> considered the reactive equivalent of Optional<T>/CompletableFuture<T> rather than of Stream<T>?
options: Mono is cardinality 0-1 (at most one element), matching Optional/Future's single-value shape, while Flux is cardinality 0-N, matching Stream
Mono cannot be composed with map or flatMap the way Optional can
Mono always blocks the calling thread until its single value arrives, unlike Optional
Mono was deprecated in Reactor 3.x in favor of using Flux for single values
explanation: The choice between Mono and Flux is dictated purely by cardinality of the result, not by habit or performance - a single entity lookup is a Mono, a list/stream of results is a Flux.

promptText: What is the defining difference between Spring MVC's and Spring WebFlux's default concurrency models?
options: MVC assigns one thread per request for its entire lifecycle, blocking on I/O; WebFlux uses a small, fixed pool of non-blocking event-loop threads that move on to other work while awaiting I/O
MVC runs on Netty while WebFlux runs on an embedded Tomcat servlet container
WebFlux can only process one HTTP request at a time per application instance
MVC threads never block; they poll for I/O completion in a tight loop instead
explanation: Spring MVC's thread-per-request model on Tomcat blocks a dedicated thread for the whole request; WebFlux's Netty event loop registers a callback and frees the thread immediately, which is the entire basis for its higher-concurrency ceiling.

promptText: Per the chapter, reactive programming provides the least benefit for which type of workload?
options: High-concurrency calls to slow, I/O-bound downstream services
CPU-bound work such as encryption or image processing
Streaming server-sent events to many long-lived clients
A live sensor feed that genuinely needs backpressure
explanation: Reactive buys concurrency headroom specifically on I/O waits; a workload that is actually limited by computation gets nothing from it, since more threads or better algorithms - not non-blocking I/O - are the real lever there.

promptText: What is the practical implication of Reactor's Mono/Flux being "cold" by default?
options: Calling .subscribe() twice on the same cold Mono/Flux re-runs the entire upstream logic independently for each subscription, including any database call or side effect
A cold publisher emits its value only once no matter how many subscribers attach to it later
Cold publishers cannot be verified with StepVerifier and require a mock Subscriber instead
Cold publishers automatically cache their result in memory after the first subscription
explanation: Most Reactor sources you build (Flux.just, Mono.fromCallable, a repository query) are cold: each subscription triggers its own independent execution, which is a classic source of bugs when developers assume a side effect only ran once.

promptText: A live price-ticker feed should show consumers only the single most recent value, discarding every intermediate update when the consumer falls behind, without unbounded memory growth. Which backpressure overflow strategy fits this best, and why is buffering the wrong choice here?
options: onBackpressureLatest - it keeps only the newest item and drops the rest, unlike onBackpressureBuffer, which queues every excess item and risks unbounded memory growth if the consumer never catches up
onBackpressureBuffer with no bound, since queuing every tick guarantees the client eventually sees the exact price history
onBackpressureError, since failing the stream the moment the consumer falls behind is the safest default for any use case
onBackpressureDrop, since dropping the newest arrivals preserves the earliest ticks, which are what a price ticker actually needs
explanation: onBackpressureLatest discards everything except the most recent item, matching the ticker's need for the current value only; unbounded Buffer risks OutOfMemoryError, and Drop keeps old values instead of the newest one a ticker actually cares about.

promptText: A developer writes `.map(id -> repo.findById(id).block())` inside a WebFlux chain. This compiles and appears to work. What is precisely wrong with it?
options: map is meant for a synchronous 1-to-1 transform; calling .block() inside it reintroduces blocking on whatever thread runs the chain, exactly the problem reactive programming exists to avoid - it should instead be flatMap without .block()
Nothing is wrong; map can safely wrap any blocking call as long as the return type matches
The code fails to compile, because map's function argument cannot invoke a method returning a Mono
map silently ignores the return value of any method call that ends in .block(), so the lookup never actually executes
explanation: The chapter calls this out directly as a disguised way of reintroducing the exact blocking-thread problem reactive was meant to solve; the rule of thumb is that any async transformation must be flatMap/concatMap, never map with an inline .block().

promptText: A chain has `.subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())` near the top and `.publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())` further down. What determines which thread each downstream operator actually executes on?
options: subscribeOn governs where the source/subscription happens (only the first one in the chain counts, regardless of position); publishOn governs execution for everything downstream of where it appears and can be repeated to hop threads multiple times
Both operators only ever affect the single operator immediately following them in the chain
publishOn governs the whole chain regardless of its position, and any subscribeOn call is ignored once a publishOn is present
Neither operator has any effect unless Schedulers.immediate() also appears somewhere in the chain
explanation: subscribeOn is position-insensitive - only the first one in a chain matters, and it governs the source; publishOn, in contrast, is position-sensitive and can appear multiple times to hop threads at different pipeline stages.

promptText: Why does pairing WebFlux with a standard Spring Data JPA repository fail to deliver full non-blocking behavior end-to-end, even though the controller layer looks fully reactive?
options: Every JPA/JDBC repository call still blocks the calling thread under the hood since JDBC's API is synchronous by design; only R2DBC gives a genuinely non-blocking path from controller to database
Spring Data JPA automatically converts itself to use R2DBC internally whenever it detects a WebFlux application context
Spring Boot refuses to start an application that mixes WebFlux and Spring Data JPA on the same classpath
WebFlux silently falls back to a Tomcat thread pool the moment any JPA repository bean is registered
explanation: Wrapping a JDBC/JPA call in a Mono doesn't make the underlying I/O non-blocking - the thread running it still blocks until the driver returns, which is exactly why R2DBC exists as a separate, genuinely non-blocking driver SPI.

promptText: Why do ThreadLocal-based mechanisms like SLF4J's MDC and Spring Security's default SecurityContextHolder break inside a Reactor pipeline, requiring Reactor Context instead?
options: A single logical subscription routinely executes across multiple different threads via subscribeOn/publishOn/async callbacks, so a value stashed in ThreadLocal before a thread-hop is invisible on the new thread afterward
ThreadLocal storage is disabled by the JVM automatically whenever reactor-core is present on the classpath
Reactor silently replaces every ThreadLocal variable in the application with a single shared static field
MDC is fundamentally incompatible with JUnit 5 and only works with JUnit 4-based reactive tests
explanation: ThreadLocal assumes one thread runs a logical operation start to finish, which a reactive chain routinely violates; Reactor's Context instead attaches state to the subscription itself, so it survives every thread hop, unlike ThreadLocal.

promptText: What is the key difference between Sinks.many().multicast() and Sinks.many().replay() regarding a subscriber that joins late?
options: multicast() only delivers emissions from the moment a subscriber joins; replay() buffers some or all history and delivers that buffered history to a new subscriber before it starts receiving live emissions
multicast() supports exactly one subscriber, exactly like unicast(); replay() supports unlimited subscribers
They behave identically at runtime; replay() is only a deprecated alias kept for backward compatibility
multicast() automatically converts itself into a cold publisher the moment its second subscriber attaches
explanation: multicast() is a hot broadcast with no history (like publish()'s late-subscriber semantics); replay() adds a bounded or unbounded history buffer so late joiners catch up before receiving live emissions.

promptText: A team schedules what they believe is a fast, in-memory cache lookup onto Schedulers.parallel() via subscribeOn, but the lookup occasionally falls through to a blocking network call. Why is this specific mistake worse in production than the same code accidentally blocking on Schedulers.boundedElastic()?
options: Schedulers.parallel() has only as many threads as CPU cores, so blocking even one of them removes a meaningful fraction of the ENTIRE application's CPU-bound processing capacity, producing gradual, non-deterministic, service-wide latency spikes rather than a contained failure
Schedulers.parallel() automatically detects any blocking call and silently redirects it to boundedElastic with zero impact
The application fails to compile whenever a blocking call is scheduled onto Schedulers.parallel()
boundedElastic() and parallel() are sized identically, so there is no meaningful difference between the two scenarios
explanation: boundedElastic() is designed to absorb many concurrently blocked threads; parallel() is a small, fixed pool sized to CPU cores that must never block, so even one rare blocking call there starves the whole application's CPU-bound work, not just the caller.

promptText: Given the assembly-time / subscription-time / execution-time model, why does a raw Reactor stack trace from a production exception often fail to show where in your own code the failing operator was declared?
options: Execution happens via generic operator classes (FluxMap, FluxFlatMap, etc.) invoked asynchronously from whatever Scheduler thread is currently running, so the trace reflects how the signal is being delivered right now, not the assembly-time call site; checkpoint() and Hooks.onOperatorDebug() exist specifically to recover that assembly-site information at a real performance cost
Java strips all stack trace frames from any method whose return type is Mono or Flux
Reactor deliberately obfuscates its internal stack traces to protect proprietary operator implementations
Exceptions thrown inside a reactive chain are always swallowed silently and therefore never produce any stack trace at all
explanation: This is a direct consequence of the assembly/execution split: by the time an exception surfaces, the trace shows Reactor's internal plumbing and whichever Scheduler happened to run it, not the sequence of your own code that assembled the chain - which is exactly the gap checkpoint()/debug mode buy back.

promptText: A chain uses `.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ...).filter(ex -> ex instanceof TimeoutException))` followed by `.onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, ex -> fallback())`. After all 3 retries are exhausted on a genuine TimeoutException, the onErrorResume handler never triggers. Why?
options: By default, Reactor's Retry.backoff wraps retry exhaustion in a RetryExhaustedException containing the original cause, so a handler keyed on TimeoutException.class no longer matches unless you unwrap it (e.g. via onRetryExhaustedThrow) or match on RetryExhaustedException instead
onErrorResume only takes effect when it is placed BEFORE retryWhen in the chain, never after it
TimeoutException cannot be matched by a filter() predicate under any retryWhen configuration
The chain silently completes with an empty Mono once retries are exhausted, without raising any error signal at all
explanation: This is the exact pitfall the chapter calls out: exhausted retries surface as RetryExhaustedException, not the original exception type, so a downstream handler keyed on the original type is skipped unless you explicitly unwrap the cause or configure onRetryExhaustedThrow to rethrow it.
